client_question: Should our dental lab buy a $250,000 3D printer for making crowns?
acceptable_recommendations: Buy the printer
key_risks: Savings assume today's crown volume; two technicians lose three weeks to training
next_steps: Confirm next year's crown orders with the largest dentists and price a service contract before signing
model_answer: Buy the printer. It costs $250,000 and saves about $70,000 a year in outsourced milling, so it pays back in about 3.6 years, well within its 7-year life. It also cuts crown turnaround from 10 days to 4, which helps win dentists' business. The main risk is that the savings assume today's crown volume, and two technicians lose three weeks to training. The next step is to confirm next year's crown orders with our largest dentists and price a service contract before signing.

client_question: Should our indoor golf-simulator studio raise its peak hourly rate from $50 to $60?

key_risks: League players, 60% of peak bookings, may push back or leave
next_steps: Raise the rate for non-league bookings first, or test for a month and track occupancy
model_answer: Raise the peak rate to $60. Peak hours are 95% booked with a waitlist most nights, so demand outruns supply at today's price, and a competing studio already charges $65. The main risk is that league players, who make up 60% of peak bookings, push back or leave. The next step is to raise the rate for non-league bookings first and track peak occupancy for a month before extending it to leagues.

The next step is to launch in Ontario with the distributor and compare sales with the projection after six months.

client_question: Should our 40-person accounting firm move to a smaller office when the lease ends?

client_question: Should our print-on-demand T-shirt company add a weekend shift to clear its order backlog?

The next step is to run it for two months and track days to ship.

client_question: Should our pasta-sauce company launch a frozen lasagna?

client_question: Should our pottery studio open a second studio or add evening classes at the current one?

client_question: Should our moving company match a new app-based rival's 20% lower prices?

key_risks: The rival moves into whole-house moves
next_steps: Track the win rate on whole-house quotes monthly

The main risk is that the rival moves into whole-house moves, so track our win rate on those quotes monthly.

client_question: Should the city extend its free downtown shuttle to the new stadium district?

client_question: Should our pest-control company buy a rival for $12M?

client_question: How should our catering company restore its profit margin?
acceptable_recommendations: Charge a premium for same-week bookings | Raise prices to match competitors' 8% increase
key_risks: Clients may push back on a rush fee or higher prices
next_steps: Model a rush fee for same-week events and test it on new bookings
model_answer: Charge a premium for same-week bookings and raise prices about 8%. Margin fell from 15% to 6% while food costs held at 30% of revenue; the cause is overtime, which doubled once same-week bookings grew to 40% of events. Our prices haven't moved in two years while competitors raised theirs 8%. The main risk is that clients balk at the rush fee. The next step is to test it on new same-week bookings for a quarter.

client_question: Should our music school switch from per-lesson pricing to a $150 monthly membership?
acceptable_recommendations: Switch to the $150 monthly membership
key_risks: Students who take fewer lessons may leave
next_steps: Offer the membership to new students first and track cancellations
model_answer: Switch to a $150 monthly membership. Students take 3.1 lessons a month at $45, about $140, so $150 keeps revenue per student, and we stop losing the 15% of booked lessons that are missed and earn nothing today. Nearby schools charge $140 to $160, so the price is in line. The main risk is that students who take fewer lessons leave. The next step is to offer it to new students first and track cancellations.

client_question: Should our UK online plant shop start shipping to Germany?

key_risks: A competitor could take the German market first
next_steps: Get quotes from a German grower to fulfil orders locally
model_answer: Don't ship to Germany from the UK. An average £35 order at a 40% margin earns £14, and shipping to Germany costs £14 plus £3 for the health certificate, so each order loses about £3. Germany's market is twice the UK's, though, so the risk is that a rival takes it while we wait. The next step is to get quotes from a German grower to fulfil orders locally, which would remove the shipping and certificate costs.

client_question: Should our cruise terminal add more check-in counters to cut waits?

client_question: Should our children's shoe brand launch a subscription that sends a new pair as feet grow?

The main risk of waiting is that a rival launches first. The next step is a 3-month pilot that tests a better fit tool and tracks cancellations.

The next step is to fix store stock counts and re-run the test.

client_question: How should our regional bus-tour company restore profit?

client_question: Should our cement plant install carbon capture for $200M?
